Let’s dive into Chapter 4: Designing Solutions That Fit the Job.
Now, once you’ve really nailed down what the real job is—what your customer’s actually trying to accomplish—the next big step is creating a solution that fits like a glove.
But here’s the thing: it’s not just about cramming in more features or tweaking performance.
You’ve got to look at the whole experience, from that very first spark of need all the way to the moment your customer feels truly satisfied.
Think about it—people aren’t just ticking off tasks. They want to feel something. Maybe it’s confidence, maybe it’s reassurance, or even a sense of belonging. Sometimes, a product that helps you feel competent or connected is every bit as valuable as one that saves you time or money.
So, how do you actually design solutions that fit the job? Let’s break it down:
First, start with a crystal-clear definition of the job.
What’s the context? What progress does your customer want to make? And what’s standing in their way?
Next, make sure your product or service covers the full spectrum of needs—not just the functional stuff, but the emotional and social sides too.
You also want your solution to slide right into your customer’s life. If it’s a hassle to adopt or use, even the best ideas can fall flat.
And don’t forget to test your prototypes with real people. Notice how well your solution actually helps them move forward, right in their own situation. Their feedback is gold.
When you approach things this way, you might end up with solutions that don’t look much like what traditional market research would predict. Sometimes, people care more about simplicity and ease than fancy features. Other times, it’s not the product itself, but how it’s delivered or supported that makes all the difference.
Let’s think about ride-sharing as an example. Sure, the basic job is getting from point A to point B. But there’s more to it. On an emotional level, riders want to feel safe, in control, maybe even respected. Socially, they might want to avoid the embarrassment of running late, or they might want to show off a certain lifestyle. The best solutions hit all those notes, making the whole experience feel natural and satisfying.
Designing for the job isn’t just about product development, either. You need your entire organization focused on helping customers make progress. That means marketing, sales, customer support, and even the behind-the-scenes processes. When everyone’s pulling in the same direction, it’s so much easier to spot ways to improve and offer a smooth, consistent experience.
And remember, this isn’t a “set it and forget it” process. As your customers’ lives evolve and new challenges pop up, the job itself might change. That’s why it’s crucial to stay close, keep listening, and keep adapting.
So, here’s the key takeaway: real innovation isn’t just luck or a gut feeling. It comes from a deep understanding of what your customer is truly trying to achieve—and building a solution that fits that job better than anything else out there. That’s how you create products and services that aren’t just useful, but genuinely meaningful and built to last.
